title: Precise vocabulary
summary: Replace vague, repetitive or exaggerated wording with accurate choices that fit the intended meaning, natural word partnerships, evidence and register.

sections.title: Choose accuracy before decoration
content: Strong vocabulary makes a meaning exact. It does not make every word longer. A familiar word that names the action accurately is stronger than an unusual synonym that changes the meaning, sounds unnatural or promises more than the evidence proves.
E7 established the paragraph's purpose, evidence and direction. Edit vocabulary only after those decisions are secure. Otherwise, polished wording can hide an unfocused claim instead of improving it.

sections.title: Move from a vague label to an observable meaning
content: Compare three versions: ‘The volunteers made things better.’ ‘The volunteers improved the return system.’ ‘The volunteers introduced labelled return trays and a reshelving rota.’ The second version narrows the result, while the third names the actions that produced it. The third is not stronger because it is longer; it is stronger because a reader can picture and check the change.

Use a precision ladder: general label → named category → observable action or feature. Climb only as high as the available evidence allows. If the notes record no measurement, do not invent a percentage to make the sentence appear precise.

sections.title: Check meaning, partnership, register and evidence
content: Test a candidate word with four questions. Meaning: does it express the intended idea? Partnership: does it combine naturally with nearby words? Register: does it suit a clear school essay rather than casual conversation or inflated ceremony? Evidence: is its strength justified? ‘Collected pupil feedback’ passes these checks more reliably than ‘got ideas’, ‘harvested opinions’ or ‘proved universal satisfaction’.

Natural word partnerships, or collocations, matter. We usually ‘collect feedback’, ‘address a problem’, ‘reach a decision’ and ‘raise a concern’. A dictionary synonym may share part of a definition without fitting the same partnership. Read the whole phrase, not the replacement word alone.

sections.title: Strengthen the load-bearing words
content: Underline vague carriers such as thing, nice, bad, good, make, do, get and very. Then ask what object, action, quality or degree the evidence actually shows. ‘Did a new shelf arrangement’ becomes ‘introduced labelled return trays’; ‘got advice’ becomes ‘collected pupil feedback’; ‘a bad system’ becomes ‘returns remained unsorted until the next session’.

Do not edit every ordinary word. Concentrate on load-bearing nouns and verbs, the evaluative words that control tone, and any phrase repeated without a clear purpose. Precise verbs often remove the need for extra adverbs: ‘examined’ is usually clearer than ‘looked at very carefully’.

sections.title: Keep useful repetition and vary only safely
content: Repetition is not automatically weak. Repeating a key term can preserve a reference chain: ‘Returned books were sorted into labelled trays. Most returns were reshelved that day.’ Replacing ‘returns’ with ‘objects’, ‘products’ or ‘literary items’ would blur the meaning merely to avoid using the same word.

Vary wording when the repeated word is vague or when a more exact term marks a genuine distinction. Keep it when it names the central concept consistently. Precision and cohesion take priority over a rule that every repeated word must receive a synonym.

sections.title: Diagnose five vocabulary failures
content: Classify a weak choice as vagueness, meaning drift, collocation error, register mismatch or overstatement. ‘Things improved’ is vague. ‘Harvested feedback’ creates meaning and collocation problems. ‘The endeavour effectuated a transformation’ is needlessly inflated for a school account. ‘Everyone always found every book immediately’ overstates what limited observations can support.

Repair the evidence-word relationship, not just the sentence surface. Replace an absolute such as ‘always’ with the bounded observation actually recorded; replace praise such as ‘amazing’ with the result that made the change useful.

sections.title: Make every important word earn its place
content: Edit a short reading-room paragraph using verified project notes. Make six decisions about vague language, exact verbs, collocation, register, cohesive repetition and evidence-bounded claims. Complete the group before viewing feedback.
